P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Generally free. There are no legal limits on private financial transfers, foreign-exchange transactions or capital movements (trade.gov). Specific rules for individuals' foreign service income were not captured.

sources.title: North Macedonia Country Commercial Guide — Trade Financing
sources.quote: There are also no legal limitations on private financial transfers, foreign exchange transactions, and capital movements.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Very likely yes. There are no legal limits on private financial transfers, foreign-exchange transactions or capital movements, and local companies may hold foreign-exchange accounts at one or more banks (trade.gov). The captured text does not explicitly cover individuals' accounts.

sources.title: North Macedonia Country Commercial Guide — Trade Financing
sources.quote: Local companies can pay for imported goods or services in foreign currencies, as they are allowed to hold a foreign exchange account in one or more banks.

P2_fcy_account.note: trade.gov (official) states no limits on private FX transactions and confirms FX accounts for companies; individuals' FX accounts are not stated explicitly in captured text.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Flat 10% on most income including self-employment. Residents are generally taxed on worldwide income (see quoted rules). Work performed while living in North Macedonia for foreign clients is generally taxable there. Sole proprietors also pay social contributions of about 28% on a base of at least 50% of the average gross salary.

sources.title: North Macedonia - Individual - Taxes on personal income
sources.quote: Macedonian tax residents are taxed on their worldwide income.

sources.title: North Macedonia - Individual - Taxes on personal income
sources.quote: As of 1 January 2023 onwards, a 10% flat tax rate is applicable on individual's income from work, self-employment income, income from royalties and industrial property rights, income from sale of own agricultural products, rental income, income from capital, capital gains, and insurance income, as well as other taxable income not categorised separately

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: VAT (DDV) is 18% (5%/10% preferential rates). Registration is mandatory once annual turnover reaches MKD 2,000,000; voluntary registration is allowed below that.

sources.quote: The standard VAT rate is 18%.

sources.title: North Macedonia VAT Guide for 2026
sources.quote: As a non-EU country, the EU's EUR 10,000 threshold does not apply — a business registers for VAT once annual turnover reaches MKD 2,000,000, with voluntary registration also allowed below that.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving). Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
